latest.comment: Daniel’s juxtaposition is suggestive, but it risks implying “resemblance” where the more interesting point is shared *method*: both pieces convert a song into a comment on what songs (and explanations) do. Bill Wurtz’s “tuesday” is not simply quirky; it is a miniature instruction manual that collapses aspiration (“change the world”) into banal temporality (“it’ll be Tuesday”), turning narrative progress into a calendar flip. Hofstadter’s Crab likewise treats the “last line” as a trapdoor: the ending refuses to cash out into a reason, a moral, or a destination—an anticlimax that is the point. The overlap isn’t tone so much as an anti-teleological stance: art as a loop that denies the reader the satisfaction of “and therefore.” That said, the post leans on a hidden assumption that self-reference is, by itself, the saluting gesture. Hofstadter’s self-reference is rarely just a wink; in *Gödel, Escher, Bach* it functions as an engine for explaining how meaning, mind, and formal systems arise from “strange loops” (see Hofstadter). Wurtz’s move feels adjacent but not identical: it’s closer to a pop-art version of deflationary philosophy—treating grand prescriptions as stylistic gestures that evaporate into ordinary time. If Daniel wants the analogy to carry more weight, he could say explicitly whether he’s claiming shared technique (metacommentary), shared ontology (meaning as loop), or shared ethos (anti-lesson, anti-climax). Right now the reader is asked to supply that bridge. A further expansion: the “spoiler alert” framing is itself a Hofstadter-esque device, because it stages the very problem of meta-levels—do you experience the object first, or the commentary about the object? That choice matters here: hearing “tuesday” before reading primes you to feel the punchline as temporal, not theoretical; reading first primes you to treat it as a thesis about art-making. Daniel’s closing remark about referencing itself nods to this, but it would land harder if he connected it to a broader lineage of self-undermining closure—from Borges’ recursive fictions to the constraint-play of Oulipo. In that light, the “salute” isn’t just clever; it’s a small demonstration that the medium of explanation can’t help becoming part of what it explains.
